outcomes: Every consumer of the CLI's workspace model — the orchestrator, extensions, and tools — sees one deterministic answer for what a target expression selects, what depends on what, and what a change reaches
The model stays a pure library: it can be read, tested and depended on without pulling in the engine that drives it
nonGoals: Workspace discovery from the filesystem, baseline resolution, and command-line flag handling, which tooling/cli owns
Scheduling and executing the jobs planned over the selected projects, which tooling/cli owns

requirements.text: A target expression resolves deterministically across exact ids, relative paths, recursive and wildcard paths, aliases, groups, unions, and subtractions: input order is preserved, a union is deduplicated, and an unknown target is an error rather than an empty selection.

Selection filters compose over the resolved targets: name and tag filters and explicit exclusions always apply, while a default-excluded tag is overridden by naming the project directly or including its tag — never the other way around.

The dependency graph answers transitive dependents, transitive dependencies, and a topological order deterministically, reports a declared cycle instead of looping, and keeps external path dependencies out of the ordering.

A changed file claims its nearest directory owner (symlinks, grouped paths canonicalized), asset, declared-input and scope-config readers, then the tasks of each that read it; a file no task reads claims nothing. Dependency edges, and contract edges whose committed contract changed, carry the tasks whose `^` reference names a source task; ordering-only edges carry none. A rebuilt extension reaches consumers for its own tasks; an unattributable claim or workspace-wide input keeps a project whole.

A project's canonical id derives from its workspace-relative path, grouped folders stay transparent so a grouped physical path resolves to the logical id, and a legacy name still resolves as a fallback.
The model module requires only protocol modules and never imports the CLI that drives it, so the boundary is enforced by the build rather than by convention.

Every dependency edge carries the manifest family it came from — a declaration, a go.mod require or replace, a package.json dependency, or a generated client's contract — without changing which edges the graph carries. A project is importable within its own scope, the nearest ancestor directory whose putnami.json contributes scope configuration; an import that leaves it is reported unless the imported project is public or a generated client, and a contract edge is always allowed.
